plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the double integral of (2x - y^2) over the triangular region R enclosed between y = -x + 1, y = x + 1, and y = 3. The figure shows the triangular region R in the xy-plane with vertices at (-2, 3), (0, 1), and (2, 3); the bounding lines y = 3 (top), y = -x + 1 (lower left), and y = x + 1 (lower right) are labeled. The y-axis divides R into two sub-regions: R1 (shaded blue, left half) and R2 (shaded yellow, right half), each with a red vertical strip indicating the direction of inner integration. The figure illustrates the decomposition of R into two type-I sub-regions required when the lower boundary changes expression across the y-axis.

interactionPlan.concept: A triangular integration region may require two Type I integrals because vertical slices have different lower boundary formulas on either side of x = 0, while Type II horizontal slices describe the whole region with one set of limits.

interactions.teaches: The learner understands that each vertical slice uses the top boundary y = 3 but needs a lower boundary formula, and that the formula changes at x = 0.
interactions.label: Edit lower boundaries for vertical slices

interactions.teaches: The learner understands that changing the slicing direction can turn a split Type I description into a single Type II description.
interactions.label: Integration order

demo_steps.title: See the triangular region
demo_steps.narration: The region R is bounded above by y = 3 and below by two different line segments, y = -x + 1 on the left and y = x + 1 on the right.

demo_steps.title: Why Type I must split
demo_steps.narration: A vertical strip always runs up to y = 3, but its lower endpoint depends on whether the strip lies left or right of the y-axis. This forces the decomposition into R1 and R2.

demo_steps.title: Connect formulas to limits
demo_steps.narration: Editing either lower boundary redraws that side of the triangle and updates the corresponding inner limits. The two sub-integrals differ only because the lower boundary changes expression at x = 0.

demo_steps.title: Switch the order
demo_steps.narration: With horizontal slices, each strip crosses the entire triangle from the left line to the right line. The same region is described by one set of Type II limits instead of two Type I pieces.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The need to split an iterated integral depends on the slicing direction, not on the region itself.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw a clean xy-plane with arrowheads, the y-axis passing through the bottom vertex of an inverted triangular region. The triangle has a horizontal top edge at y = 3 from x = -2 to x = 2, a lower-left diagonal edge descending to the vertex (0, 1), and a lower-right diagonal edge rising from that vertex. Use thick cyan boundary lines. In the Type I view, shade the left half light blue and label it R1, shade the right half light yellow and label it R2, and place one red vertical strip in each half. Show equation labels near their corresponding boundaries: y = 3 above the top edge, y = -x + 1 near the left diagonal, and y = x + 1 near the right diagonal. In the Type II view, keep the same triangle but remove the internal split emphasis and show horizontal blue slices spanning from the left boundary to the right boundary. Keep the formulas and limit displays visually tied to the current slicing direction.

- equation_input for the two lower boundary equations: two fields pre-filled with "-x + 1" (left, for R1) and "x + 1" (right, for R2); when the learner edits either, the corresponding boundary line redraws, the shaded sub-regions R1 and R2 update, and the inner integral limits display — shows directly how the lower boundary formula changing expression at x=0 is what forces the decomposition into two sub-integrals
- toggle between Type I (vertical slices, R1 + R2 split with red strips) and Type II (horizontal slices, single region with blue horizontal strips and limits x from -(y-1) to (y-1)) — teaches that switching integration order eliminates the need to decompose R
